name: Bit Game (Easy Version)
description: This is the easy version of this problem. The only difference is that you need to output the winner of the game in this version, and the number of stones in each pile are fixed. You must solve both versions to be able to hack. Alice and Bob are playing a familiar game where they take turns removing stones from $$$n$$$ piles. Initially, there are $$$x_i$$$ stones in the $$$i$$$-th pile, and it has an associated value $$$a_i$$$. A player can take $$$d$$$ stones away from the $$$i$$$-th pile if and only if both of the following conditions are met: $$$1 \le d \le a_i$$$, and $$$x \, \& \, d = d$$$, where $$$x$$$ is the current number of stones in the $$$i$$$-th pile and $$$\&$$$ denotes the bitwise AND operation . The player who cannot make a move loses, and Alice goes first. You're given the $$$a_i$$$ and $$$x_i$$$ values for each pile, please determine who will win the game if both players play optimally.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 1000$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^4$$$) — the number of piles. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \lt 2^{30}$$$). The third line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i \lt 2^{30}$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^4$$$.
output_specification: Print a single line with the winner's name. If Alice wins, print " Alice ", otherwise print " Bob " (without quotes).

subsubtopic: 472. Grundy Number and Basic Game Theory
approach_summary: Compute Sprague-Grundy values g(u) = mex({g(v) : u -> v}). Game state is winning iff XOR sum of independent game components is non-zero.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2027E1 — Bit Game (Easy Version) [472. Grundy Number and Basic Game Theory]
topic_editorial.summary: Impartial game theory via Sprague-Grundy theorem.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Any finite, impartial game under normal play convention is equivalent to a one-pile game of Nim with pile size equal to its Grundy value $g(u) = \text{mex}(\{g(v) : u \to v\})$. A compound game of independent subgames is winning for the first player if and only if $\bigoplus_{i} g_i \ne 0$.
